Ospray
OS-pray
noun
The Authorized Version’s spelling of osprey, from the Old French ospres and ultimately the Latin ossifraga, “bone-breaker”; a great fish-hawk, rendering the Hebrew 'ozniyyah.

Biblical Definition

The ospray is a great fish-hawk, a bird of hooked beak and grappling talons that drops upon its prey out of the air. It stands third in the roll of forbidden fowls, in the company of the largest raptors: “the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray” (Lev 11:13; cf. Deu 14:12). The chapter opens that list with a word heavier than dislike — “these are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls” — and the birds that head it share one trait: they live by seizing life and by feeding on blood. That is the key to the whole category. Israel was a people forbidden the blood, for the life of the flesh is in the blood and God had given it upon the altar to make atonement; and a bird that ate blood as its daily bread could never come to the table of a people whose whole religion turned on blood reserved to God. The law was a shadow, “but the body is of Christ” (Col 2:17). The prohibition was not squeamishness about hawks. It was a standing sermon that life belongs to God, that blood is not common, and that the only blood which may be taken and lived upon is the blood God Himself appointed — the blood of His Son, given for many for the remission of sins.

Webster 1828 Definition

A great fish-hawk of hooked beak and talons; third in the roll of fowls held in abomination.

expand to see more

OSPRAY, the sea-eagle or fish-hawk, a large bird of prey that feeds upon fish.

From Old French ospres, from Latin ossifraga, “bone-breaker.”

It seizes its prey by dropping upon it from a height with the talons.

Named with the eagle and the ossifrage as an abomination (Lev 11:13).

Repeated in Moses’ second recital of the law (Deu 14:12).

Key Scripture

Lev 11:13 — "And these are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls; they shall not be eaten, they are an abomination: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray,"

Deu 14:12 — "But these are they of which ye shall not eat: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray,"

Lev 20:25 — "Ye shall therefore put difference between clean beasts and unclean, and between unclean fowls and clean: and ye shall not make your souls abominable by beast, or by fowl, or by any manner of living thing that creepeth on the ground, which I have separated from you as unclean."

Col 2:17 — "Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ."

Modern Corruption

The birds of prey are moralised into emblems of cruelty; the law makes them a lesson about blood, and the lesson terminates on the cross.

expand to see more

The easy misreading is to preach the ospray as a picture of the rapacious man — predatory, grasping, a warning against greed. That is a sermon the text does not give. The bird is not blamed for being what God made it; the eagle’s talons and the hawk’s stoop are the Creator’s handiwork, and the same Lord who forbade the ospray to Israel’s table feeds the young ravens which cry. To moralise the creature is to lose the type. The birds head the abomination list because of what they consume, and what they consume is blood; and blood, in Israel’s whole economy, was the one thing reserved absolutely to God.

The doctrine to recover is that the ceremonial law was not arbitrary and is not obsolete in its meaning, only in its form. Every one of these ordinances was “a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.” The shadow said: life is God’s, blood is holy, no man takes it for himself. The body said: the Son of God poured out His blood, and now the command is not touch it not but drink ye all of it. What was forbidden to the whole nation is commanded to the whole church, because the blood in question is no longer taken by a predator but given by a Redeemer. The ospray on the list and the cup on the table are two ends of one doctrine.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The bone-breaker — a great fish-hawk, third among the fowls held in abomination.

expand to see more

Ospray — the AV spelling of osprey; Latin ossifraga, “bone-breaker.”

Renders the Hebrew 'ozniyyah, a great bird of prey.

Named third in the abomination list, after the eagle and the ossifrage (Lev 11:13).

Birds of prey head the list because they live upon blood.

The prohibition guarded the doctrine that blood belongs to God (Lev 20:25).

Usage

"The ospray heads the list with the eagle: birds that live by blood."

"The bird is not blamed for its talons; the law is teaching Israel about blood."

"A shadow of things to come — and the body is of Christ."
